decks.title: Accounting Application of Electronic Spreadsheet — Part 1: Spreadsheet Basics, Formatting and Functions
goals: Explain what an electronic spreadsheet is and state its utility, merits and demerits in accounting
Create, rename, copy and move worksheets, refer to another sheet, enter, navigate and save data
Format cells and set up pages for previewing and printing
Write formulas with relative, absolute and named references, and use SUM, AVERAGE, percentages, date functions and IF; freeze panes

slides.heading: Accounting Application of Electronic Spreadsheet
slides.body_md: Part 1 — what an **electronic spreadsheet** is, how **workbooks and worksheets** are organised, how to **format and print**, and how **formulas and functions** do an accountant’s arithmetic. Software is described generically; every firm is imagined.

nodes.label: What a spreadsheet is; merits and demerits

visual.alt: Route map of Part 1: what a spreadsheet is with its merits and demerits, workbooks and worksheets, formatting and printing, formulas and references, functions including average, percentage, dates and IF, and freezing panes
visual.caption: Part 1 at a glance

slides.narration: This chapter is about using an electronic spreadsheet for accounting work. In this first part we learn what a spreadsheet is and where it helps and falls short, how a workbook holds many worksheets, how to format and print a sheet, and how formulas and functions such as sum, average, the date functions and if do the arithmetic for us. An imagined stationery shop, Pakhawaj Paper Mart, is our example.

slides.heading: What a spreadsheet is, and its utility

rows: Allowances, provident fund, tax and net pay by formulas copied down for every employee
Profit on sales and slab commission by IF; totals and averages by functions
Debit and credit totals with an agreement check; balances by SUMIF
Due dates and days overdue from date arithmetic; lists sorted and filtered
Change one rate and see every result update
Formatted statements printed or drawn as charts from the same cells

visual.alt: Table of accounting jobs a spreadsheet helps with: payroll, sales and commission, journal and ledger balances, debtors and due dates, budgets and what-if analysis, and reports and charts

slides.narration: An electronic spreadsheet is a grid of columns and rows. Each cell can hold a label, a number or a formula, and every formula recalculates by itself when a figure it uses changes. That makes it a natural tool for accounts: payroll, sales and commission, a journal with its totals, debtors and due dates, budgets that test new rates, and reports and charts drawn from the same figures.

slides.heading: Merits and demerits

rows: Automatic recalculation when any figure changes
A wrong reference or formula spreads errors silently
What-if analysis by changing one input cell
No built-in double-entry control: unbalanced entries are accepted
Formulas can be overwritten by typed figures
Weak security; no record of who changed what
Unsuited to very large volumes and many users at once
Compact storage; easy correction and sharing
Needs training; files can be lost without backups

visual.alt: Table of merits of electronic spreadsheets, such as automatic recalculation, what-if analysis, functions, formatting, sorting and charts, reuse and easy correction, against demerits, such as silent formula errors, no double-entry control, overwritten formulas, weak security, limits on volume and the need for training and backups

slides.narration: The merits are speed and accuracy from automatic recalculation, what-if analysis by changing one input, ready-made functions, neat formatting, sorting and charts, and designs that can be reused every month. The demerits matter too. A spreadsheet has no double-entry control, so an unbalanced entry is accepted. A wrong reference spreads errors silently, typed figures can overwrite formulas, and security is weak.

slides.narration: Think about what checks a spreadsheet makes on its own, compared with accounting software.

slides.narration: Here is the window of a typical spreadsheet program. The title bar shows the workbook name, and the menu and toolbar hold the commands. Columns carry letters, rows carry numbers, and the tabs at the bottom switch between the worksheets of the workbook.

slides.heading: Workbooks, worksheets, cells and ranges

rows: The file that holds one or more sheets
One grid of columns and rows, with a tab
Columns lettered A … Z, AA, AB …; rows numbered 1, 2, 3 …
Where a column meets a row; named column then row
A rectangular block written first cell:last cell

visual.alt: Table of spreadsheet terms: workbook, worksheet, columns and rows, cell and address, range, and a reference to another sheet, each with an example from Pakhawaj Paper Mart

slides.narration: A workbook is the file, and it holds one or more worksheets, each with its own tab. Columns run from A to Z, then A A, A B and so on, and rows are numbered. A cell is named by its column and row. A range is a block written as its first and last cells with a colon between them. To use a cell on another sheet, write the sheet name, an exclamation mark and the cell.

slides.heading: Entering data, navigating and saving

rows: Select a cell, type, press Enter (moves down) or Tab (moves right); text aligns left and numbers right by default
Double-click it (or press F2) and correct; Delete clears it
Drag the fill handle: April, May, June … or 1, 2, 3 … or copy a formula down
Arrow keys; Ctrl + Home to A1; Ctrl + arrow to the edge of the data; type an address in the name box
Save keeps the same file; Save As makes a copy with a new name, place or format
Open an existing workbook; close it after saving

visual.alt: Table of everyday tasks: entering data, editing a cell, filling a series with the fill handle, navigating with keys and the name box, saving with Save and Save As, and opening and closing workbooks

slides.narration: To enter data, select a cell, type and press enter to move down or tab to move right. Text lines up on the left and numbers on the right. The fill handle continues a series such as April, May and June, or copies a formula down. Control and home takes you to cell A one. Save keeps the same file, while save as makes a copy under a new name.

visual.alt: Table of actions on worksheets: insert, rename, delete, move, copy, and move or copy to another workbook, with how each is done and the result

slides.narration: Right-click a sheet tab to insert, rename, delete, move or copy a worksheet. Moving changes only the sheet’s position, so formulas that refer to it still work. Copying leaves the original in place and makes a duplicate with the same entries and formulas. With the move or copy command, a sheet can also be moved or copied into another open workbook.

slides.heading: Worked example 1: a quarterly summary from three sheets
slides.body_md: Pakhawaj Paper Mart (imagined, Krishnanagar) keeps sheets named April, May and June; B6 of each totals four product lines. A fifth sheet, Summary, brings the three totals together.

visual.alt: Summary sheet of Pakhawaj Paper Mart: B two to B four bring in the totals from the April, May and June sheets, B five adds them to 8,93,350, and B six gives the monthly average
visual.caption: Each month sheet totals its four product lines in B6, for example `=SUM(B2:B5)` on the April sheet.

slides.narration: On the summary sheet, B two refers to cell B six of the April sheet, B three to the same cell on the May sheet, and B four to June. The sum function in B five adds them to rupees eight lakh ninety-three thousand three hundred fifty, and B six rounds the average month to two decimal places. If a figure on any month’s sheet changes, the summary updates by itself.

slides.heading: Formatting cells
bullets: A date is stored as a **count of days**, so dates can be subtracted.

visual.alt: Table showing one stored value under different formats: general, comma style with Indian grouping, two decimals, a percentage with one decimal, two date formats, and the date shown as a general number of days
visual.caption: A format changes only the display; formulas use the stored value. A date is stored as a count of days.

slides.narration: Formatting changes how a value looks, never the value itself. The same number can show plainly, in the comma style with Indian grouping, with two decimals or as a percentage. A date is stored as a count of days, which is why it can show as an ordinary number and why one date can be subtracted from another. Formulas always use the full stored value.

slides.heading: Formatting tools for an accounts sheet

rows: Alignment, wrap text, merge and centre
Long headings fit; the title spans the table
Comma style for rupees, percentages, dates
Auto-fit so no amount shows as ####
Highlight, say, overdue amounts in red

visual.alt: Table of formatting tools and their use: fonts, alignment with wrap text and merge and centre, number formats, column width, borders and fill colours, and conditional formatting

slides.narration: Use bold and larger fonts for titles and headings. Merge and centre spreads a title across the table, and wrap text lets a long heading run onto two lines. Apply the comma style to rupee columns and percentage or date formats where needed. Widen columns so that amounts do not show as hash marks, add borders and fill colours, and use conditional formatting to highlight overdue amounts.

slides.heading: Page set-up, preview and printing

rows: Portrait for long narrow sheets; landscape for wide ones
A4 or legal; narrow margins fit more
Fit to one page wide, or a percentage of normal size
Repeats heading rows (or columns) on every page
Firm name, page number, date on each page
Shows the pages exactly as they will print, before printing

visual.alt: Table of page set-up and printing options: orientation, paper size and margins, scaling, print area, print titles, header and footer, and print preview

slides.narration: Before printing, open the page set-up. Choose landscape for a wide sheet, set the paper size and margins, and scale the sheet to fit one page wide. Set a print area if only part of the sheet is needed, and print titles so that the heading row repeats on every page. Add a header or footer with the firm’s name and page numbers, then check everything in print preview.

slides.heading: Formulas and operators

rows: Multiply and divide before add and subtract

visual.alt: Table of operators with B one holding forty-eight thousand and B two thirty-six thousand: adding, subtracting, multiplying, dividing, brackets giving a margin of twenty-five, the order of operations, comparison and joining text
visual.caption: B1 = 48,000 (sales) and B2 = 36,000 (cost). Every formula begins with =.

slides.narration: A formula always begins with an equals sign. Brackets are worked first, then multiplication and division, then addition and subtraction. So sales minus twice the cost is not the same as sales minus cost, doubled. Comparison operators give true or false, which the if function uses, and the ampersand joins pieces of text. Always refer to cells rather than typing the figures again.

slides.heading: Relative, absolute and named references

headers: When the formula is copied one row down
rows: Becomes B3: it moves with the formula
A dollar sign before the column letter and before the row number
A dollar sign before only the column letter or only the row number
A name such as NetTotal or DARate given to one cell

visual.alt: Table of kinds of cell reference, relative, absolute, mixed, named cells and references to another sheet, with how each is written and what happens when the formula is copied
visual.caption: This course shows locked references as named cells; in your answers you may write either.

slides.narration: When a formula is copied, a relative reference moves with it, which is why one formula typed in row two can be copied to every row. A rate or total kept in a single cell must not move. Lock it by putting a dollar sign before both the column letter and the row number, or give the cell a name such as net total. A named cell never moves.

slides.narration: Functions are ready-made formulas. Sum adds a range and average divides by the number of figures, skipping empty cells. Max and min find the largest and smallest. Round fixes the decimals, half away from zero. The if function chooses between two results by a test, and and or join tests. Count if counts cells that meet a condition. Date builds a date, and day, month and year take one apart.

slides.narration: Row two is typed once and copied down. The amount multiplies quantity by rate. The discount uses the if function: exam pads, at rupees eighteen thousand, fall below the limit and get nothing, while the other three lines get five per cent, rounded to the rupee. Net amounts total rupees ninety-nine thousand five hundred ten. The share divides each net amount by the total, which is named so that the formula copies safely.

slides.heading: Worked example 3: due dates and days overdue

visual.alt: Credit register of Ghatam Glassware as on thirtieth September: due date is invoice date plus credit days, days overdue are fifty, eleven, three and zero, and a nested if labels each customer follow up, overdue or not due
visual.caption: B1, named AsOn, holds 30-09-2026. Overdue amount by SUMIF: ₹1,39,550.

slides.narration: Because dates are counts of days, the due date is simply the invoice date plus the credit days. The cell named as on holds the thirtieth of September. If that date is later than the due date, the difference gives the days overdue; otherwise the if returns zero. Saha Caterers are fifty days late, so a nested if says follow up. Kundu Sweets are not yet due.

slides.narration: To sum up: a spreadsheet holds labels, numbers and formulas in cells and recalculates by itself, but it has no accounting controls of its own. A workbook holds many sheets, which can be renamed, moved and copied, and referred to by name. Formats change only the display. Formulas follow the order of operations, references are relative, absolute or named, and functions handle totals, averages, tests and dates.

slides.heading: Exam tips
bullets: Write every formula with **cell references**, starting with **=**, and state what the cell **shows**.
Lock or **name** a rate or total cell before copying a formula.
AVERAGE **skips blank cells**; a typed zero is counted.
Freeze panes is for the **screen**; print titles are for **paper**.
slides.narration: Write each formula with cell references, begin it with an equals sign and say what the cell will show. Name or lock any single rate or total before copying a formula. Use brackets whenever something must be added before it is multiplied. Remember that average skips blank cells but counts a typed zero, and that freezing panes affects only the screen, not the printout.

slides.body_md: Part 2 — four **applications** named in the syllabus (payroll, sales and commission, student marks, journal), then **charts** and a spreadsheet **database** that can be sorted, filtered and queried.

slides.narration: Now we put the tools of part one to work. We build a payroll sheet, a sales sheet with salesmen’s commission, a marks sheet with results and grades, and a journal with its totals and ledger balances. Then we present figures as charts, and treat a list of debtors as a small database that we sort, filter and question. Every firm, school and figure is imagined.

slides.heading: Designing an accounting application

nodes.label: Inputs in their own cells (rates named)

visual.alt: Steps to design an accounting application in a spreadsheet: inputs in their own named cells, a formula written once in the first row, copied down, totals and checks, then formatting, printing and charts
visual.caption: Change a rate cell and every row updates.

slides.narration: Every application follows the same plan. Put each input, such as a rate, in its own cell and give it a name. Write the formula once, in the first row of the table, and copy it down. Add totals and checks with the sum and if functions. Finally format, print or chart the result. When a rate changes, every row updates by itself.

slides.heading: The parts of a payroll

rows: 10% of gross above ₹50,000 (simplified rule for this course)

visual.alt: Table of payroll components: basic pay, dearness allowance, house rent allowance, travelling allowance, city compensatory allowance, provident fund, income tax deducted and net pay, with the rule and formula used in the Sarangi sheet
visual.caption: Rates sit in N2:N7, named DARate, HRARate, CCA, PFRate, TaxLimit and TaxRate.

slides.narration: Gross pay is basic pay plus allowances. Dearness allowance offsets rising prices and house rent allowance helps with rent, both as percentages of basic pay here. Travelling allowance depends on the basic pay, set by an if test, and city compensatory allowance is a flat sum. Provident fund, at twelve per cent of basic plus dearness allowance, and income tax are deducted to give net pay.

slides.heading: Worked example 1: allowances and gross pay
slides.body_md: Sarangi Spice Exports (imagined, Raiganj), April 2026: five employees; rates in named cells. TA: ₹1,600 if basic is below ₹30,000, else ₹2,400.

visual.alt: Payroll of five employees of Sarangi Spice Exports: basic pay, dearness allowance at forty per cent, house rent allowance at twenty per cent, travelling allowance by an if test, city compensatory allowance and gross pay totalling three lakh two hundred rupees
visual.caption: Row 2 formulas: C2 `=ROUND(B2*DARate,0)`; D2 `=ROUND(B2*HRARate,0)`; E2 `=IF(B2<30000,1600,2400)`; G2 `=SUM(B2:F2)`.

slides.narration: Row two holds the formulas, copied down to row six. For Chumki, with basic pay of rupees thirty-two thousand, dearness allowance is rupees twelve thousand eight hundred and house rent allowance rupees six thousand four hundred. Her basic pay is not below the limit, so travelling allowance is rupees two thousand four hundred. Adding city compensatory allowance, her gross pay is rupees fifty-four thousand six hundred. The gross pay of all five comes to rupees three lakh two hundred.

slides.heading: Worked example 1 continued: deductions and net pay

visual.alt: Deductions and net pay at Sarangi Spice Exports: provident fund on basic plus dearness allowance, income tax only on gross pay above fifty thousand, and total net pay of two lakh sixty-four thousand one hundred ninety-six rupees
visual.caption: Row 2 formulas: H2 `=ROUND((B2+C2)*PFRate,0)`; I2 `=IF(G2>TaxLimit,ROUND((G2-TaxLimit)*TaxRate,0),0)`; J2 `=H2+I2`; K2 `=G2-J2`.

slides.narration: Provident fund is twelve per cent of basic plus dearness allowance, so Chumki’s is rupees five thousand three hundred seventy-six. Under this course’s simplified rule, tax is ten per cent of gross pay above fifty thousand: rupees four hundred sixty for her. Her net pay is rupees forty-eight thousand seven hundred sixty-four. Aparupa and Subhojit earn less than the limit and pay no tax. Total net pay is rupees two lakh sixty-four thousand one hundred ninety-six.

slides.narration: A sales sheet lists each salesman’s sales and cost of goods sold. Profit is sales minus cost, and profit on sales divides profit by sales. Commission often has slabs, such as two per cent on sales up to the target and five per cent on the excess, which one if formula handles. A second if labels whether the target was met, and count if counts those who met it.

slides.heading: Worked example 2: Shehnai Home Appliances

visual.caption: G9 counts the salesmen who met the target with COUNTIF.

slides.narration: Srijita sold rupees four lakh five thousand. The first two per cent applies to the target, six thousand rupees, and five per cent to the excess of one lakh five thousand, five thousand two hundred and fifty more, so her commission is rupees eleven thousand two hundred fifty. Brishti fell short, so she gets two per cent of all her sales. Total commission is rupees thirty-seven thousand nine hundred eighty, and three of the five met the target.

slides.heading: Worked example 3: a student marks sheet
slides.body_md: Ektara Shiksha Niketan (imagined school, Bolpur): four papers out of 100; pass with at least 33 in every paper; grade A from 75%, B from 60%, C from 45%, else D; E for a student who fails.

visual.alt: Marks sheet of Ektara Shiksha Niketan for five students in four papers: totals, percentages, results by the lowest mark and grades by a nested if; Payel fails on one paper although her percentage is above the pass mark
visual.caption: Row 2: `=SUM(B2:E2)`; `=ROUND(F2/4,2)`; `=IF(MIN(B2:E2)>=33,"Pass","Fail")`; grade `=IF(H2="Fail","E",IF(G2>=75,"A",IF(G2>=60,"B",IF(G2>=45,"C","D"))))`.

slides.narration: Total uses the sum function, and the percentage divides by four. The result tests the lowest mark, not the percentage: Payel’s percentage is above thirty-three, but she scored thirty in one paper, so she fails and her grade is E. The grade formula checks the result first and then the cut-offs from the highest down. Count if shows that four students passed.

slides.heading: Worked example 4: a journal and ledger balances
slides.body_md: Dilruba Dairy (imagined, Balurghat) keeps its May 2026 journal with one line for each account: the debit line, then the credit line.

visual.alt: Journal of Dilruba Dairy for May in a spreadsheet: six entries of two lines each, debit and credit totals of ten lakh twenty thousand rupees and a check showing agreed
visual.caption: C14 `=SUM(C2:C13)`; C15 `=IF(C14=D14,"Agreed","Check entries")` → Agreed.

slides.narration: Each entry takes two lines, so the debit and credit columns can each be added with the sum function. Both total rupees ten lakh twenty thousand, and an if formula compares them and shows agreed. The spreadsheet would not stop an unbalanced entry by itself; this check is what catches one.

slides.narration: The conditional sum function adds only the rows that meet a condition. To find the cash balance, it adds the debit amounts on lines whose account is cash and takes away the credit amounts on those lines. Cash has a balance of rupees twelve thousand and the bank rupees one lakh ninety thousand. Change any journal line and the balances change with it.

sections.heading: 1. The electronic spreadsheet: meaning, utility, merits and demerits
sections.body_md:
An **electronic spreadsheet** is a program that arranges a **worksheet** of columns (A, B, C …) and rows (1, 2, 3 …); each **cell** holds a label, a value or a **formula**, and formulas **recalculate automatically** when a figure they use changes.

**Utility in accounting:** payroll; sales, profit and commission; journals with totals and ledger balances; debtors with due dates; budgets and what-if analysis; depreciation and loan schedules; reports and charts.

**Merits:** automatic recalculation and accuracy; what-if analysis; ready-made functions; formatting, sorting, filtering and charts; one design reused every period; compact storage, easy correction and sharing.

**Demerits:** no built-in double-entry control; silent spread of a wrong reference or formula; formulas can be overwritten; weak security and no record of changes; unsuited to very large volumes or many users; needs training and backups.

key_terms.definition_md: A program of cells in columns and rows holding labels, values and formulas that recalculate automatically.
Changing an input cell to see at once how the results change.

rows: Allowances, provident fund, tax and net pay by formulas copied down for every employee
Profit on sales and slab commission by IF; totals and averages by functions
Debit and credit totals with an agreement check; balances by SUMIF
Due dates and days overdue from date arithmetic; lists sorted and filtered
Change one rate and see every result update
Formatted statements printed or drawn as charts from the same cells

sections.heading: 2. Workbooks and worksheets: entering, saving, navigating, copying and moving
sections.body_md:
A **workbook** is the file; it holds **worksheets**, each with a tab. Columns run A … Z, AA, AB …; a **cell address** is column then row (B3); a **range** is written first cell:last cell (B2:E9).

**Entering and editing:** type and press Enter (down) or Tab (right); text aligns left, numbers right; double-click or F2 to edit; the **fill handle** continues series and copies formulas.

**Navigating:** arrow keys; Ctrl + Home (to A1); Ctrl + arrow (edge of the data); the name box (go to an address).

**Saving:** Save overwrites the same file; **Save As** creates a copy with a new name, place or format.

**Worksheets:** insert, rename, delete, move (references still work), copy (a duplicate with the same formulas), and move or copy into another open workbook. A **reference to another sheet** is the sheet name, an exclamation mark and the cell: `=May!B6`.

key_terms.definition_md: The spreadsheet file, holding one or more worksheets.
A rectangular block of cells, written first cell:last cell.
Saves a copy under a new name, place or format, leaving the original file unchanged.

sections.heading: 3. Formatting, previewing and printing
sections.body_md:
**Formatting cells:** font, size, bold and colour; alignment, **wrap text**, **merge and centre**; **number formats** (comma style, decimals, percentage, currency, dates such as dd-mm-yyyy or dd-mmm-yyyy); column width and row height (auto-fit; #### means the column is too narrow); borders and fill colours; conditional formatting.

A format changes **only the display**; formulas use the stored value (two cells showing 10.00 can add to 20.01). A date is stored as a count of days, so dates can be added to and subtracted.

**Page set-up and printing:** orientation (portrait or **landscape**); paper size and margins; scaling (fit to one page wide); **print area**; **print titles** (rows to repeat at the top of each page); header and footer; gridlines; **print preview** before printing.

sections.heading: 4. Formulas and functions: arithmetic, average, percentage, dates, IF; freezing panes
sections.body_md:
A **formula** begins with **=**. Order: brackets, then × and ÷, then + and −. Comparison operators (> < >= <= = <>) give TRUE or FALSE; & joins text.

**References:** **relative** (B2) moves when copied; **absolute** (a dollar sign before the column letter and before the row number) and **named** cells (DARate, NetTotal) do not; **mixed** locks one part.

**Functions:** `SUM`, `AVERAGE` (skips blanks), `MAX`, `MIN`, `COUNT`, `COUNTIF`, `ROUND(number, places)`; percentage = part ÷ whole × 100, often `=ROUND(B3/B7*100,2)`; `IF(test, value if true, value if false)`, nested IF for slabs and grades, with `AND` / `OR` for joint tests; dates: `DATE(year, month, day)`, `DAY`, `MONTH`, `YEAR`, `TODAY()`; date − date = days, date + days = a later date.

**Freeze panes:** select the cell below the rows and right of the columns to keep; those rows and columns stay on screen while scrolling (screen only; use print titles for paper).

sections.heading: 5. Payroll
sections.body_md:
**Gross pay** = basic pay + DA + HRA + TA + CCA (+ other allowances). **Net pay** = gross pay − deductions (provident fund, income tax deducted at source, others).

**Design:** employees in rows; rates and limits in their own named cells (DARate, HRARate, PFRate, TaxLimit …); formulas in row 2 copied down; a totals row.

**Formula patterns (Sarangi Spice Exports):** DA `=ROUND(B2*DARate,0)`; HRA `=ROUND(B2*HRARate,0)`; TA `=IF(B2<30000,1600,2400)`; gross `=SUM(B2:F2)`; PF `=ROUND((B2+C2)*PFRate,0)`; income tax `=IF(G2>TaxLimit,ROUND((G2-TaxLimit)*TaxRate,0),0)` (a simplified rule for this course; real income-tax rules are annual and slab-based); net `=G2-J2`.

Check: net pay + deductions = gross pay, row by row and in total.

sections.body_md:
**Sales sheet:** profit = sales − cost of goods sold; profit on sales (%) = `ROUND(profit/sales*100,2)` (on cost would be a mark-up). **Commission** by IF: a single rate by a test (`=IF(B4>=Target,ROUND(B4*3%,0),ROUND(B4*1%,0))`) or **slabs** (2% up to the target, 5% on the excess: `=IF(B4>Target,ROUND(Target*2%+(B4-Target)*5%,0),ROUND(B4*2%,0))`); a status label by IF; `COUNTIF` for the number who met the target.

sections.heading: 7. Journal in a spreadsheet
sections.body_md:
**Layout:** Date, Account, Debit, Credit, with one line per account in each entry (debit line first, then the credit line; a narration column may follow).

**Totals and check:** `=SUM(C2:C13)` and `=SUM(D2:D13)`; `=IF(C14=D14,"Agreed","Check entries")`; the difference `=C14-D14` helps trace a slip (a figure keyed as 1,800 instead of 18,000 leaves 16,200).

**Ledger balances by SUMIF:** `=SUMIF(B2:B13,"Cash",C2:C13)-SUMIF(B2:B13,"Cash",D2:D13)` gives the cash balance (positive = debit balance).

The spreadsheet itself accepts an unbalanced entry; only the check built by the user catches it.

sections.heading: 8. Charts, and the spreadsheet as a database: sorting, querying and filtering
sections.body_md:
**Charts:** select the data with its labels, insert a chart, add a title, axis titles, legend and data labels, and format it; it redraws when the figures change. Column or bar to **compare**; line for a **trend**; pie for **parts of one whole**; stacked column for parts across periods; scatter for two related measures.

**Database (list):** one heading row of **field names**; each row a **record**; no blank rows or columns; one kind of entry per column.

**Sort:** select the whole list; sort by one or more keys, ascending (A to Z, smallest first) or descending.

**Filter:** hides records that fail the conditions (AutoFilter, custom conditions such as Amount ≥ 40,000 **and** Status = Due); nothing is deleted; clear the filter to see all.

**Query:** a question answered from the list, by a filter or by `COUNTIF` / `SUMIF`, for example `=SUMIF(E2:E9,"Due",D2:D9)`.

notes.exam_tips_md:
**Common mistakes**
- Formula without **=**, or with figures typed in instead of **cell references**.
- Copying a formula that uses a single rate or total cell without **naming or locking** it.
- Forgetting **brackets**: `=B2+B3*B4` is not `=(B2+B3)*B4`.
- Taking AVERAGE as total ÷ all cells when some cells are **blank**.
- Treating a **format** as if it changed the value.
- Provident fund on gross pay instead of the stated base; adding tax to gross pay.
- Applying the higher commission rate to the **whole** sales in a slab scheme.
- Deciding pass or fail on the **percentage** when the rule is every paper.
- Sorting **one column** of a list; thinking a filter deletes records.
- Using freeze panes to repeat headings on **printed** pages.

**How marks are usually split**
- 1 mark: a term, a function, a format, a reference, or one formula result.
- 2 marks: two formulas with values, or two points explained.
- 3 marks: a short sheet (three formulas with values), three merits or steps.
- 5 marks: a full application in parts (for example 2 + 3): payroll, sales and commission, marks, a journal with SUMIF, or a sort–filter–query problem. Formulas and values carry separate marks.

**Figures in SOYL practice** are imagined; your paper will give its own rates and rules.

questions.stem_md: Mr Animesh Kar keeps the accounts of an imagined stationery shop, Kartal Copy House, Tamluk, on a computer. Which description fits the electronic spreadsheet he uses?

A database that accepts only vouchers in which debits equal credits

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (b)** A grid of rows and columns whose cells hold text, numbers and formulas that recalculate when a figure changes. Sorting of records in ascending order
Printing of gridlines and headings
Automatic recalculation of every formula that depends on the changed cell

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (d)** Automatic recalculation of every formula that depends on the changed cell. D2 multiplies the quantity by the rate and D4 adds the amounts, so both depend on C2; the rise of ₹2,400 flows through without retyping anything.

questions.solution_md: **Correct option: (a)** A wrong cell reference in one formula can carry an error silently into every total that uses it. A spreadsheet does exactly what its formulas say; it has no built-in double-entry control, so a faulty formula or an overwritten cell can go unnoticed.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. **Automatic recalculation and accuracy:** formulas add, multiply and take percentages by themselves; when one figure changes, every total that depends on it is updated, so there are no arithmetical slips.
2. **What-if analysis:** the effect of a new price, wage rate or discount can be seen at once by changing one input cell.
3. **Reuse and presentation:** a sheet designed once (a payroll or sales sheet) can be copied for every month; figures can be formatted, sorted, filtered, charted and printed neatly.
4. *(Also accepted)* Large amounts of figures held compactly and found quickly; easy correction without overwriting; sheets shared or exported to other programs.

questions.stem_md: An imagined engineering firm, Esraj Engineering, wants to keep its entire double-entry books in spreadsheets instead of accounting software. State two demerits of spreadsheets it should keep in mind.
questions.solution_md: Contrast what accounting software enforces with what a spreadsheet leaves to the user.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. **No built-in accounting control:** a spreadsheet does not insist that debits equal credits or that accounts exist; an unbalanced or misposted entry is accepted unless the user builds checks.
2. **Errors and security:** a wrong reference or an overwritten formula spreads errors silently, and sheets can be changed by anyone who opens the file, with no record of who changed what.
3. *(Also accepted)* Unsuited to very large numbers of transactions or many users at once; depends on the skill of whoever designs the formulas; files can be lost without backups.

questions.stem_md: The payroll sheet of an imagined bakery, Bansuri Bakery, has the title "Salary sheet for April 2026" in A1 and long column headings such as "House rent allowance (₹)" in row 3, spread over columns A to K. 2. **Headings:** select row 3, turn on wrap text so long headings run onto two lines within the column width, make them bold, centre them and add borders (and a light fill colour) so they stand apart from the figures.

questions.stem_md: The sales register of an imagined pharmacy chain, Chimta Chemists, has 12 columns and 140 rows. Printed as it is, it spills on to extra pages sideways and only the first page shows the headings. Explain three page set-up or printing steps that will give a clean printout.
questions.solution_md: Deal with the width, the headings on every page and checking before printing.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. **Orientation and scaling:** choose landscape orientation and scale the sheet to fit one page wide (letting the length run over several pages), reducing margins if needed.
2. **Print titles and print area:** set row 1 (the headings) as rows to repeat at the top so every page carries them, and set the print area to the register only, leaving out rough work.
3. **Preview before printing:** use print preview to check page breaks, headers and footers (for example the firm’s name and page numbers), and gridlines, then print.
